lesson.title: Remember the Maine: A Mystery That Pushed a Nation to War
lesson.summary: The explosion that destroyed the USS Maine in Havana harbor in February 1898 killed over 250 American sailors and became the rallying cry for war with Spain, even though its true cause remains disputed to this day.
lesson.body:
In January 1898 the United States sent the battleship USS Maine to Havana, ostensibly to protect American citizens and interests during the unrest of the Cuban rebellion against Spain, though the visit also carried an implicit show of force. On the night of February 15, 1898, a massive explosion tore through the ship as it sat at anchor in Havana harbor, and the Maine sank quickly, killing 266 of the roughly 355 men aboard.

American newspapers, particularly Hearst's New York Journal, moved immediately to blame Spain, running dramatic headlines and diagrams purporting to show a Spanish mine detonating beneath the hull, even before any real investigation had taken place. The rallying cry Remember the Maine, to hell with Spain spread quickly and became a driving force behind the public demand for war that followed within the Spanish-American War just two months later. A US Navy Court of Inquiry, working quickly and under intense public pressure, concluded in 1898 that an external mine had caused the explosion, a finding that fit the prevailing mood but was reached without the kind of technical evidence that would satisfy investigators today.

It is important to be honest about what is actually known. Later inquiries, including a 1911 investigation and a technical review commissioned in the 1970s by Admiral Hyman Rickover, raised serious doubts about the mine theory, suggesting that the explosion may have originated inside the ship, possibly from a fire in a coal bunker igniting an adjacent ammunition magazine, a known hazard on warships of that design. No investigation, past or present, has produced conclusive proof of what actually happened, and historians today generally treat the cause of the Maine's destruction as an unresolved question rather than a settled case of Spanish sabotage. What is certain is the political effect: whether or not Spain was responsible, the disaster and the press coverage surrounding it turned American public opinion decisively toward war within weeks.
